units.translation: This verb has a double spelling: the older γίνομαι [I become], sometimes written γείνομαι [I am born], the other γίγνομαι [I become]. On both forms see the Thesaurus vol. 2 p. 620-621. Here it will be enough to note that the Attic tragic poets and other old Attic writers consistently used the form γίγνομαι [I become], as the testimonies of grammarians and examples from inscriptions confirm. Although this form is often preserved in the manuscripts of the tragic poets and other old Attic writers, especially in the Platonic manuscripts, nevertheless the scribes not infrequently introduced the other form γίνομαι [I become], which the grammarians assign to the common dialect; this happened in Sophocles in the Medicean codex in six places, in Aeschylus Pr. 319, Sept. 379, 398, 439, Pers. 708, [Ag. 623 in the apographs, for M lacks this part of the play], Eum. 136, 216, 750, Suppl. 936. But γίγνεται [it becomes] at Suppl. 476, 793. The same applies to γινώσκω [I know] and γιγνώσκω [I know], which in M is consistently γινώσκω [I know], but in Sophocles is written sometimes one way, sometimes γιγνώσκω [I know]. Aeschylus used these forms of the verb γίγνομαι [I become]: present γίγνομαι [I become], imperfect ἐγιγνόμην [I was becoming], perfect middle γέγονα [I have become], passive γεγένημαι [I have been made], aorist middle ἐγενόμην [I became], imperative γενοῦ [become!], optative γενοίμην [may I become] (and this indeed most often), subjunctive γένωμαι [I may become], γένῃ [you may become], γένηται [he may become], γένησθε [you may become], infinitive γενέσθαι [to become], future γενήσομαι [I will become]. The aorist form ἔγεντο [he became], which epic and lyric poets sometimes used, Arnaldus wanted to restore in Sept. 779: ἔγεντο μέλεος ἀθλίων [he became the object of care for the wretched] instead of ἐγένετο [he became], because in the antistrophe v. 786 a pure iambus is read: ἐφῆκεν ἐπικότους τροφᾶς [he sent forth wrathful nourishments].
Examples of common usage are these:
with words interpolated for οἷα πείσεται [what he will suffer], as it seems; on which I have spoken under the word ἄνοια [folly].

in the apograph ἐπεὶ γένοιτ' [when it might happen] for ἐπιγένοιτ' [when it might come upon], which is in M, in an interpolated passage, on which I have spoken in the Preface to the fifth Leipzig edition p. LXXXIX.
i.e. ἔνδον φρενῶν γενοῦ [be within your senses], contain or restrain yourself.
by tmesis for συγγενοῦ [be born with, be akin to].
[γενέσθαι [to become], on which see under the word τίνω [I pay, I atone].]

Among these there are many examples where the substantive verb could be used, although even in such places it does not lose its proper notion of becoming. Thus Sept. 1045: ἄθαπτος δ᾽ οὗτος οὐ γενήσεται [but this man will not become unburied], which is not said simply for ἔσται [he will be], but means 'it will not come about that he lies unburied.'
The expression τις or τί γένωμαι [who or what may I become] means 'who or what am I to become,' 'what is to become of me,'
[But Eum. 789 and 819 τί ῥέξω; γένωμαι [what shall I do? May I become], rightly γελῶμαι [may I be mocked] Tyrwhitt.]
γίγνεσθαι [to become] with the dative of the person, which in such places can often be rendered by the verb 'to befall'.
